title: Coalition Politics

cards.h: Coalitions: from crisis to a normal way to govern
cards.b:
No party won a Lok Sabha majority between 1989 and 2009. Governments were formed by coalitions, and states had them even earlier. The 2024 election returned the country to a coalition government at the Centre: the BJP won 240 seats, short of the 272 needed, and the NDA formed the government with allies such as the TDP and JD(U).

A coalition is a government made of two or more parties that agree to share office and a programme. In parliamentary systems, it is born when no party has a majority.

Examiners ask: are coalitions good or bad for India? Do they cause instability? How did the constitution and courts adapt? Your answer should combine theory, a timeline and constitutional rules.

Key points: the Janata Party was a merger, not a coalition. In 1989, V.P. Singh's National Front governed with the BJP and Left giving outside support. The 1996 Vajpayee government lasted 13 days. The 1998 NDA government lost a vote of confidence by one vote in April 1999 after the AIADMK withdrew support, but the 1999 NDA, with over twenty parties, completed a full term. UPA I (2004) lost Left support in 2008 over the Indo-US nuclear deal.

William Riker, The Theory of Political Coalitions (1962)

The size principle: parties form coalitions just large enough to win, since extra partners only dilute rewards. Minimum winning coalitions are most likely.

Robert Axelrod, Conflict of Interest (1970)

Parties prefer partners close in ideology, forming minimal connected winning coalitions.

Why India often breaks these rules

Indian coalitions are often oversized (NDA 1999 with 24 parties) or minority governments (Rao 1991). Reasons: pre-poll alliances at constituency level, state-level interests, and the benefit of the winning alliance in first-past-the-post. E. Sridharan has argued that coalition politics is a product of India's parliamentary federalism, with state parties as key players.

Another key notion: coalitions can be pre-poll (seat-sharing before the election, favoured under FPTP) or post-poll (formed after results). Outside support is when a party backs a government without joining it.

cards.h: How coalitions run: programmes and managing partners
cards.b:
• Common Minimum Programme: UPA's 2004 CMP; the NDA's National Agenda for Governance (1999). These set out what partners agree on and leave out contentious items such as Ayodhya (for the NDA).
  • Coordination bodies: NDA's convener, UPA's chairperson and the National Advisory Council (2004-14) chaired by Sonia Gandhi.
  • "Coalition dharma": Vajpayee's phrase for respecting allies' interests.
  • Cabinet size: the 91st Amendment (2003) capped the Council of Ministers at 15% of the House (Article 75(1A)). It stopped jumbo cabinets built to please allies.
  • Collective responsibility (Article 75(3)) is tested when ministers belong to different parties. Parties have sometimes treated it flexibly.

Managing allies shaped policy: regional parties gained railway, agriculture or telecom ministries, and states won funds.

cards.h: The law of defection and the Governor's role
cards.b:
Instability came from defection ("Aya Ram, Gaya Ram" in Haryana, 1967). The 52nd Amendment (1985) added the Tenth Schedule: a legislator is disqualified if he voluntarily gives up party membership or defies a whip on a vote. The 91st Amendment (2003) removed the exemption for splits, leaving only a two-thirds merger exemption. The Speaker decides. In Kihoto Hollohan (1992), the Supreme Court upheld the law and said the Speaker's decision is open to judicial review. In Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020), it asked Speakers to decide petitions within three months.

In a hung House, who is invited? The Sarkaria Commission advised: first, the pre-poll alliance with a majority; then the largest party or group. S.R. Bommai (1994) says the floor of the House, not the Governor's view, tests the majority. In Subhash Desai (May 2023), on Maharashtra's 2022 crisis, the Court held that the Governor had no basis to call a floor test and that the Speaker's whip appointment was illegal, but did not restore the previous government since the Chief Minister had resigned.

Arguments for:

  • They include many regions and social groups; policy needs wider consent.
  • They force consultation and restrain dominance.
  • Rao (1991-96) delivered the economic reforms from a minority; Vajpayee pursued disinvestment and the Golden Quadrilateral; UPA I introduced MGNREGA (2005), RTI (2005) and RTE (2009).

Arguments against:

  • Bargaining by small allies for portfolios, and the difficulty of acting against a partner's ministers. Critics linked UPA II's corruption scandals to this.
  • Delay in decisions; 'policy paralysis' charges for the second UPA.
  • Instability in 1989-99 (six Prime Ministers in ten years).
  • Opportunism, horse-trading and defections at state level (resort politics).

Verdict: the issue is less coalition itself than a weak party culture and the lack of binding programmes. India's stability from 1999 to 2014 shows coalitions can last.

Coalition politics changed Centre-state relations. Regional parties in the ruling alliance could bargain for their states, so the Centre could no longer ignore them.

  • Use of Article 356 fell sharply after Bommai (1994) and the coalition era began.
  • The United Front's Common Minimum Programme (1996) promised greater devolution of funds to states.
  • States won more say in finance: the Finance Commission share of central taxes rose from 32% (13th FC) to 42% (14th FC) and settled at 41% (15th and 16th FC).
  • The Inter-State Council was revived (1990) and later the GST Council (2016) made states partners in tax decisions.

Scholars therefore link the coalition era to the rise of cooperative and bargaining federalism. With a single-party majority from 2014 to 2024, many saw a return to a stronger Centre, while in 2024 the dependence on allies returned.

cards.h: Reform proposals: stability without losing representation
cards.b:
• Constructive vote of no-confidence (as in Germany): a government can be removed only if the House simultaneously elects a new leader. The Law Commission's 170th Report (1999) and the NCRWC (2002) both recommended it.
  • Fixed terms: proposals for fixed Lok Sabha terms, linked to the debate on simultaneous elections.
  • Stricter defection law: taking decisions out of the Speaker's hands. The NCRWC and Election Commission suggested the President or Governor, on the Election Commission's advice, should decide disqualification.
  • Pre-poll alliance rules: give the pre-poll alliance priority when forming a government.
  • Party law: regulate internal democracy and funding.

Opponents of reform argue that stability must not be bought by silencing smaller voices. Most commentators accept that coalitions are a feature of a plural society.

• Kerala: the LDF and UDF alternate; in 2026 the UDF returned.
  • West Bengal: the Left Front ruled for 34 years (1977-2011) with the CPI(M) dominating partners.
  • Bihar: the NDA's 2025 landslide shows the power of a well-managed pre-poll alliance.
  • Maharashtra: the 2019 post-poll crisis, the Maha Vikas Aghadi, the 2022 Shiv Sena split and the 2024 Mahayuti win.
  • Union, 2024: BJP 240 and NDA 293. The TDP (16) and JD(U) (12) hold key positions. The INDIA bloc, formed in 2023, won 234 but has found state-level seat-sharing difficult.

Remember the lesson: when alliances are pre-poll and ideological, the government is stable; when they are post-poll and opportunistic, it is fragile.
